# The three learning paradigms 🎓 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## How do machines learn?
### Three different approaches

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- AI algorithms learn patterns from data
- But [what kind of data]{.alert} and [what kind of feedback]{.alert}?
  1. [Supervised learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning): learn from labelled examples (last lecture)
  2. [Unsupervised learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unsupervised_learning): find structure in unlabelled data
  3. [Reinforcement learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning): learn from rewards and punishments
- Your choice depends on [the data you have]{.alert} and [the goal you want]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Learning paradigms overview and examples](figures/learning-types.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/learning-types.png"}

Source: [Medium](https://luigi-bungaro.medium.com/what-is-machine-learning-short-and-complete-guide-9e474a89396a)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Supervised learning 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What is supervised learning?
### Learning from examples with answers

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Supervised learning]{.alert}: learn from labelled examples
- Training data: input-output pairs $(x_i, y_i)$
- Goal: learn a function $f$ such that $f(x) \approx y$
- The "supervision" is a [teacher]{.alert} giving the correct answers: the [known labels]{.alert}
- [Most common paradigm]{.alert} in real-world applications
- Examples:
  - Email → Spam/Not spam
  - Image → Cat/Dog/Bird
  - Patient data → Disease risk
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![A hard classification problem 😂](figures/muffins.jpeg){width="75%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/muffins.jpeg"}

Source: [Memedroid (!)](https://pt.memedroid.com/memes/detail/4155054/Confusing-machine-learning?refGallery=random&page=109&goComments=1)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Classification vs regression
### The two main supervised tasks

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**Classification** 🏷️

- Predict a [discrete category]{.alert}
- Binary: Yes/No, Spam/Ham
- Multi-class: Cat/Dog/Bird/Fish
- Output: class label (or probabilities)
- Examples:
  - Fraud detection
  - Disease diagnosis
  - Sentiment analysis
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**Regression** 📈

- Predict a [continuous value]{.alert} (a number)
- Examples:
  - House price prediction
  - Stock price forecasting
  - Temperature prediction
  - Age estimation from photo
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
:::{style="margin-top: 20px; text-align: center;"}
> The same algorithm family often handles both tasks with minor modifications!
:::
:::
:::

## Linear models
### The simplest supervised learners

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Linear regression]{.alert}: predict y as a weighted sum of features

$$\hat{y} = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \ldots + w_n x_n$$

- Learn weights $w$ that minimise prediction error
- [Logistic regression]{.alert}: classification via the [sigmoid function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmoid_function)

$$P(y=1|x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w_0 + w_1 x_1 + \ldots)}}$$

- Simple, interpretable, fast to train
- Works well when relationships are roughly linear
- A [strong baseline]{.alert} before trying complex models
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -70px;"}
[![Linear regression fits a line](figures/linear-regression.gif){width="70%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/linear-regression.gif"}

Source: [Medium](https://medium.com/swlh/from-animation-to-intuition-linear-regression-and-logistic-regression-f641a31e1caf)

[![A logistic function converts a line into a curve](figures/logistic-function.png){width="60%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/logistic-function.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_function)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Decision trees
### Learning rules from data

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Decision trees]{.alert}: learn a hierarchy of yes/no questions
- Each node splits the data on a feature; leaves hold the predictions
- Easy to interpret: "If income > $50k AND age > 30, then approve loan"
- Capture [non-linear relationships]{.alert}
- Prone to [overfitting]{.alert} (memorising training data)
- Fix: [random forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_forest) combine many trees
  - Each tree sees different data/features
  - Averaging their predictions raises accuracy
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Decision tree structure](figures/decision-tree.gif){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/decision-tree.gif"}

Source: [Medium](https://medium.com/towards-data-engineering/100-days-of-machine-learning-on-databricks-day-63-decision-trees-5d4df25b194f)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Neural networks for supervised learning
### Learning complex patterns

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Neural networks]{.alert}: layers of interconnected nodes, each transforming the input
- Learn [arbitrarily complex]{.alert} functions
- Deep networks (many layers) = [deep learning]{.alert}
- Need [more data]{.alert} than simpler models
- Less interpretable ("black box")
- State-of-the-art for:
  - Image classification (CNNs)
  - Speech recognition
  - Natural language processing
- [Backpropagation]{.alert} makes training possible (lecture 02)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Neural network architecture](figures/neural-network.gif){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/neural-network.gif"}

Source: [3Blue1Brown](https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/neural-networks)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The bias-variance trade-off
### Too simple or too complex?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Every model makes errors!]{.alert} Two sources:
- [Bias]{.alert}: error from oversimplified assumptions
  - Underfitting: model too simple, misses real patterns
- [Variance]{.alert}: error from sensitivity to training data
  - Overfitting: model too complex, memorises noise and fails on new data

$$\text{Total Error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Noise}$$

- [Trade-off]{.alert}: reducing one often increases the other
- Goal: find the [sweet spot]{.alert} where total error is smallest
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -30px;"}
[![Bias-variance trade-off](figures/bias-variance.gif){width="80%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/bias-variance.gif"}

Source: [Vizuara](https://www.vizuaranewsletter.com/p/e91)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Cross-validation
### Testing your model properly

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- A single train/test split can be [misleading]{.alert}: it ignores [random variation]{.alert}
- [Cross-validation]{.alert}: use multiple train/test splits
- [K-fold CV]{.alert}: split the data into K parts
  - Train on K-1 folds, test on 1 fold
  - Repeat K times, rotating the test fold
  - Average the results
- Benefits:
  - [Every data point]{.alert} is tested once, so the estimate is more reliable
  - Helps detect overfitting
- Common choice: K = 5 or K = 10
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![5-fold cross-validation](figures/cross-validation.gif){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/cross-validation.gif"}

Source: [Vizuara](https://www.vizuaranewsletter.com/p/f6a)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Unsupervised learning 🔍 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What is unsupervised learning?
### Finding structure without labels

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Unsupervised learning]{.alert}: learn from data without labels
- No correct answers given. The goal is to find [hidden structure]{.alert}
- Like learning [without a teacher]{.alert}
- Why use it?
  - [Labels are expensive]{.alert}: experts have to make them
  - Labels sometimes [don't exist]{.alert} ("How many customer types?")
  - [Exploration]{.alert}: understand the data before modelling
  - [Pre-training]{.alert}: learn representations, then fine-tune
- Two questions to ask first: are there natural groups? Can the data be compressed?
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Unsupervised learning finds structure](figures/unsupervised-learning.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/unsupervised-learning.png"}

Source: [University of Cambridge](https://docs.science.ai.cam.ac.uk/ai-core-concepts/unsupervised-learning/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Clustering
### Grouping similar data points

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Clustering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluster_analysis): partition data into groups (clusters)
- Points in a cluster are [similar]{.alert}, points across clusters are [dissimilar]{.alert}
- [K-means](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-means_clustering), the most popular algorithm:
  1. Choose K cluster centres at random
  2. Assign each point to the nearest centre
  3. Move each centre to the mean of its points
  4. Repeat until convergence
- [Hierarchical clustering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchical_clustering): builds dendrograms without pre-specifying K
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -50px;"}
**Real-world uses:**

| Domain | Application |
|--------|-------------|
| Marketing | Customer segmentation |
| Biology | Cell types, disease subtypes |
| Finance | Fraud detection |
| Healthcare | Patient risk groups |

[![K-means clustering](figures/kmeans2.gif){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/kmeans2.gif"}

Source: [Machine Learning CoBan](https://machinelearningcoban.com/2017/01/01/kmeans/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Dimensionality reduction
### Compressing information

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Curse of dimensionality]{.alert}: high-dimensional data is hard to work with
  - Distances lose meaning, data needs grow exponentially, plots become impossible
- [Dimensionality reduction]{.alert}: find a lower-dimensional representation
- Keep the structure, drop the noise
- [Linear]{.alert}: PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
- [Non-linear]{.alert}: t-SNE, UMAP
- Uses: visualisation, preprocessing, compression
- [Cool example]{.alert}, more in [lecture 06](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci101/lectures/lecture-06/06-language.html): <https://projector.tensorflow.org/>
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Reducing dimensions while preserving structure](figures/dimensionality-reduction.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/dimensionality-reduction.png"}

Source: [Medium](https://muhammadtaha01.medium.com/dimensionality-reduction-in-machine-learning-46d45747eaee)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Dimensionality reduction techniques
### PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Linear:** [PCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_component_analysis) (Principal Component Analysis)

- Find the directions of [maximum variance]{.alert}
- Keep the top K components to reduce dimensions
- Fast, well understood, keeps global structure
- Limitation: only captures linear relationships

**Non-linear:** [t-SNE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-distributed_stochastic_neighbor_embedding) and [UMAP](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)

- Keep [local structure]{.alert}: nearby points stay nearby
- Excellent for [visualisation]{.alert}
- Reveal clusters that PCA misses
- Caution: cluster sizes and distances can mislead
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Principal Component Analysis](figures/pca.gif){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/pca.gif"}

Source: [Vizuara](https://www.vizuaranewsletter.com/p/understanding-principal-component)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Reinforcement learning 🎮 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What is reinforcement learning?
### Learning from interaction

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Reinforcement learning (RL)]{.alert}: learn by trial and error
- An [agent]{.alert} interacts with an [environment]{.alert}
- It takes [actions]{.alert} and receives [rewards]{.alert} (or punishments)
- Goal: learn a [policy]{.alert} that maximises cumulative reward
- Like training a dog (or kids!): [reward good behaviour!]{.alert}
- [Unlike supervised]{.alert}: no "correct" action is given
- [Unlike unsupervised]{.alert}: there IS a goal (maximise reward)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -20px;"}
[![The RL loop](figures/rl-loop.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/rl-loop.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Key concepts in RL

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 32px;"}

| Concept | Definition | Example (Chess) |
|---------|------------|-----------------|
| **Agent** | The learner/decision-maker | The chess-playing AI |
| **Environment** | What the agent interacts with | The chess board and opponent |
| **State** | Current situation | Board position |
| **Action** | What the agent can do | Move a piece |
| **Reward** | Feedback signal | +1 win, -1 lose, 0 otherwise |
| **Policy** | Strategy: state → action | "In this position, move queen" |
| **Value** | Expected future reward from a state | How good is this position? |

:::{style="font-size: 22px;"}
> Fun fact: [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen) once said he ["can't beat his phone in chess"](https://www.firstpost.com/sports/chess/magnus-carlsen-on-playing-against-chess-computer-engine-difficulty-joe-rogan-podcast-13867015.html). RL really works! 😅
:::
:::

## The exploration-exploitation trade-off
### Should you try something new or stick with what works?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 25px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Exploration]{.alert}: try new actions to find better strategies
- [Exploitation]{.alert}: use known good actions to maximise reward
- Too much exploration wastes time on bad actions
- Too much exploitation misses better strategies
- Restaurant choice: exploit your favourite, or explore a new one (might be better!)
- To [balance both]{.alert}, a common approach is [ε-greedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epsilon-greedy), explore with probability ε, also called [multi-armed bandit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-armed_bandit)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Exploration vs exploitation](figures/exploration-exploitation.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/exploration-exploitation.png"}

Source: [Lilian Weng](https://lilianweng.github.io/lil-log/2018/01/23/the-multi-armed-bandit-problem-and-its-solutions.html)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Q-learning
### Learning action values

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 19px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Q-learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q-learning): learn which action is best in each situation
- Keep a [score card]{.alert}: $Q(s, a)$ = "How good is action $a$ in state $s$?"
- The agent learns by doing:
  1. Try an action, see the reward → *"Go right... hit a wall, ouch!"*
  2. Update the score → *"Going right here is bad"*
  3. Repeat thousands of times → *"Eventually: always go left here!"*

**The update rule:**
$$\text{New Score} = \text{Old Score} + \text{Small Correction}$$

- [Policy]{.alert}: always pick the action with the highest score
- [Cool example]{.alert}: (Poor) Albert learns to walk: <https://youtu.be/L_4BPjLBF4E?&t=137>
- [Even better]{.alert}: [DeepMind's AlphaGo](https://deepmind.google/research/alphago/): <https://youtu.be/WXuK6gekU1Y>
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/q-learning01.gif){width="70%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/q-learning01.gif"}
[![](figures/q-learning02.gif){width="70%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/q-learning02.gif"}

Source: [Medium](https://medium.com/data-science/getting-started-with-reinforcement-q-learning-77499b1766b6)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## RLHF: RL for language models
### From AlphaGo to ChatGPT

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [RLHF]{.alert}: [Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback](https://openai.com/index/learning-from-human-preferences/)
- [Key to ChatGPT's success!]{.alert}
- Process:
  1. Train a base LLM on text (supervised)
  2. Collect human preferences on model outputs
  3. Train a [reward model]{.alert} on those preferences
  4. Use RL to optimise the LLM for that reward
- Why it works:
  - No formula can specify a "good response"
  - Humans find it easier to [compare]{.alert} responses
- More here: <https://openai.com/index/learning-from-human-preferences/>
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![RLHF pipeline](figures/rlhf.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/rlhf.png"}

Source: [Simform](https://www.simform.com/blog/reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Jailbreaking RLHF
### If you can make it, you can jailbreak it!

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=70%}
- With the right prompt, you can make an LLM do (almost) anything
- More art than science (as most things in AI are), but fun!
- [I'm not encouraging you to jailbreak anything]{.alert}: you may get permanently banned from LLMs, or worse
- [Pliny the Liberator](https://x.com/elder_plinius) has jailbroken pretty much every LLM he could reach 😂: <https://pliny.gg/>
- [Claude Sonnet](https://claude.ai) teaching how to produce drugs: <https://x.com/elder_plinius/status/1972885831955484830>
:::

:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -20px;"}
[![](figures/pliny.jpg){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/pliny.jpg"}

Source: [Pliny the Liberator](https://pliny.gg/)
:::

:::

## AI safety
### Making sure AI does what we actually mean

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 27px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Alignment problem]{.alert}: make models do what we *mean*, not what we literally *say*
- [Specification gaming]{.alert}: models find perverse ways to maximise rewards (e.g., [reward hacking]{.alert})
- [Scalable oversight]{.alert}: how to supervise models more capable than their human evaluators
- [Red teaming]{.alert}: hunt for vulnerabilities and [jailbreaks]{.alert} before others do
- [Build safety into training]{.alert}, don't bolt it on later
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"}
[![AI alignment](figures/ai-safety.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/ai-safety.png"}

Source: NanoBanana
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Comparing the three paradigms 📊 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Side-by-side comparison

:::{style="margin-top: 70px; font-size: 30px;"}

| | [Supervised]{.alert} | [Unsupervised]{.alert} | [Reinforcement]{.alert} |
|---|----------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Data** | Labelled (X, y) | Unlabelled (X) | States, actions, rewards |
| **Goal** | Predict y from X | Find structure | Maximise reward |
| **Feedback** | Correct answers | None | Reward signal |
| **Analogy** | With a teacher | Exploring alone | Trial and error |
| **Evaluation** | Against known labels | Internal metrics | Cumulative reward |
| **Examples** | Spam detection, diagnosis | Customer segments | Game playing, robotics |
| **Difficulty** | Medium (if labels exist) | Hard to evaluate | Hard to train |

:::

# Summary 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Main takeaways

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 30px;"}

- [Three paradigms]{.alert}: Supervised (labels), unsupervised (no labels), reinforcement (rewards)

- [Supervised learning]{.alert} is most common: Learn from labelled examples to predict

- The [bias-variance trade-off]{.alert}: Simple models underfit, complex models overfit

- [Unsupervised learning]{.alert} discovers hidden structure: Clustering, dimensionality reduction

- [Reinforcement learning]{.alert} learns from interaction: Exploration vs exploitation

- [RLHF]{.alert} powers modern LLMs like ChatGPT: RL to align with human preferences
:::
